title: Week 8B: Transformations
text:
Reading a log-y model

m_log <- lm(log(uninsured) ~ poverty + bachelors + median_age, data = cty)
round(coef(m_log), 4)

(Intercept)     poverty   bachelors  median_age 
     3.0849      0.0157     -0.0155     -0.0210 

round(100 * (exp(coef(m_log)[-1]) - 1), 1)

   poverty  bachelors median_age 
       1.6       -1.5       -2.1 



“Adjusting for education and median age, each additional percentage point of poverty is associated with about 1.6% higher uninsured rate (multiplicatively), among US counties in 2019”
Careful: that is 1.6 percent of the rate (8% becomes 8.13%), not 1.6 percentage points

title: Week 8B: Transformations
text:
When does log(y) help?

Right skew in y: log pulls in the long tail
Multiplicative structure: effects that plausibly act in percent terms (incomes, rates, concentrations, counts of anything that grows)
Variance rising with the mean: the funnel-shaped residual plot from Week 6; log often stabilizes it
Here the gain is modest and honest: R^2 moves from 0.262 (raw) to 0.272 (log), but the residuals lose most of their right skew. Transformations are for validity, not for chasing R^2

title: Week 8B: Transformations
text:
Box-Cox: a formal guide
Box-Cox considers the family y^{(\lambda)} = (y^\lambda - 1)/\lambda, with \lambda = 0 meaning \log y, and profiles the likelihood over \lambda:

MASS::boxcox(lm(uninsured ~ poverty + bachelors + median_age, data = cty),
             lambda = seq(-0.5, 1, 0.05))

title: Week 8B: Transformations
text:
The Box-Cox profile










Dotted lines: the peak and its 95% interval, which covers 0 but not 1

title: Week 8B: Transformations
text:
Choosing lambda pragmatically
For our model the likelihood peaks at \hat\lambda \approx 0.07 with a 95% interval of roughly (-0.03, 0.16).

Nobody can interpret y^{0.07}. The interval covers 0, so use the log
Snap to interpretable values: 1 (nothing), 1/2 (square root), 0 (log), -1 (reciprocal)
If the interval covers 1, resist transforming at all: interpretability beats optimality
Box-Cox needs y > 0; it advises, it does not command

title: Week 8B: Transformations
text:
Transforming predictors: log(x)
Density spans 0.1 to almost 70,000 people per sq mi: a linear term lets NYC set the slope for rural Kansas.

den <- county_health |> drop_na(uninsured, density) |> filter(density > 0)
m_raw <- lm(uninsured ~ density, data = den)
m_logx <- lm(uninsured ~ log(density), data = den)
c(r2_raw = summary(m_raw)$r.squared, r2_logx = summary(m_logx)$r.squared)

     r2_raw     r2_logx 
0.002217547 0.054179990 



R^2 jumps from 0.002 to 0.054: the raw scale saw almost nothing
Coefficient -0.67: each doubling of density goes with about a -0.47 point change in uninsured rate (coefficient \times \log 2)

title: Week 8B: Transformations
Week 8B: Transformations
text:
Polynomials: curvature without logs

lm(uninsured ~ poly(median_age, 2), data = county_health)


Adds curvature while keeping y and x on their original scales
Always keep lower-order terms when you include higher ones
Danger zone: polynomial tails do absurd things outside the data range; never extrapolate a quadratic
Rule of thumb: log for skew and multiplicative stories, polynomials for genuine humps and dips

title: Week 8B: Transformations
text:
Cautions before you transform

Back-transformation: a log-y prediction e^{\hat y} estimates the median of y, not the mean; say which you report
Zeros: \log 0 = -\infty. One county has density 0, one has uninsured 0. Dropping a known handful is honest if disclosed; \log(y + 1) changes the question and depends on units
Interpretation debt: pay it back in the write-up; if you cannot explain the coefficient to a health department, reconsider
Transform to fix structure (skew, curvature, funnels), not to nudge a p-value

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
Three kinds of unusual observations
Three different ways one observation can be unusual:

Leverage: unusual in the predictors (an extreme x-profile); it has the potential to move the fit
Outlier: unusual in the response given its predictors (a big residual)
Influence: actually moves the fit; roughly outlier \times leverage


They are separate diagnoses: a point can be any combination. Today’s classic example has one of each flavor.

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
The classic: 50 countries’ savings rates
savings (faraway package): averages over 1960-1970 for 50 countries.

sr: personal savings rate (% of disposable income)
pop15, pop75: % of population under 15 and over 75
dpi: per-capita disposable income; ddpi: its growth rate (%)
We regress sr on all four: n = 50, p = 5 coefficients, so every observation matters

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
Leverage: the hat values
\hat y = Hy; the diagonal entries h_i of H say how much observation i’s own response pulls on its own fitted value.

h_i depends only on the predictors, not on y_i
Average is p/n = 5/50 = 0.10; a common flag is h_i > 2p/n = 0.20
High leverage comes from an unusual predictor combination


h <- hatvalues(g)
sort(h, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]

        Libya United States         Japan 
    0.5314568     0.3336880     0.2233099

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
Leverage: half-normal plot

halfnorm(h, labs = row.names(savings), ylab = "Leverage")









Libya sits far above the pack; the United States is a distant second

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
Why is Libya out there?

savings[c("Libya", "United States", "Japan"), ]

                 sr pop15 pop75     dpi  ddpi
Libya          8.89 43.69  2.07  123.58 16.71
United States  7.56 29.81  3.43 4001.89  2.45
Japan         21.10 27.01  1.91 1257.28  8.21

summary(savings$ddpi)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.220   2.002   3.000   3.758   4.478  16.710 



Libya, h = 0.53: half its fit comes from its own response
Culprit: ddpi = 16.7 vs a median of 3.0 (an oil boom)
The United States (0.33) is extreme on dpi: rich, but on-trend
Leverage is exposure, not a crime: what does the fit do with it?

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
Outliers: scaled residuals
Raw residuals have unequal variances, \sigma^2 (1 - h_i), so we scale:

Standardized: r_i = e_i / (\hat\sigma \sqrt{1 - h_i})
Studentized: same, but \hat\sigma is re-estimated without i, so an outlier cannot inflate its own yardstick


sort(abs(rstudent(g)), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]

     Zambia       Chile Philippines 
   2.853558    2.313429    1.863826 



Zambia leads at 2.85. Big? We searched 50 residuals, so a plain t cutoff cheats

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
The Bonferroni idea
Testing all 50 countries at level 0.05 needs a per-country level of 0.05/50:

qt(1 - 0.05 / (2 * 50), df = 50 - 5 - 1)

[1] 3.525801



Critical value about 3.53; Zambia’s 2.85 does not reach it: no formal outlier in this dataset
Lesson: with many observations, some residual always looks large; the Bonferroni correction keeps you from crying wolf
An outlier that survives the correction deserves investigation, not deletion

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
Influence: Cook’s distance
How much do all fitted values move if we delete i and refit?
D_i = \frac{r_i^2}{p} \cdot \frac{h_i}{1 - h_i}
(big residual) \times (big leverage) = influence.

ck <- cooks.distance(g)
sort(ck, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]

     Libya      Japan     Zambia 
0.26807042 0.14281625 0.09663275 



Libya: modest residual, huge leverage, D = 0.27: most influential

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
Cook’s distance: half-normal plot

halfnorm(ck, 3, labs = row.names(savings), ylab = "Cook's distance")









Libya’s D is about twice Japan’s, the next largest

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
Refit without Libya

g_nolibya <- lm(sr ~ pop15 + pop75 + dpi + ddpi, data = savings,
                subset = row.names(savings) != "Libya")
round(rbind(full = coef(g), no_Libya = coef(g_nolibya)), 4)

         (Intercept)   pop15   pop75    dpi   ddpi
full         28.5661 -0.4612 -1.6915 -3e-04 0.4097
no_Libya     24.5240 -0.3914 -1.2809 -3e-04 0.6103



The ddpi coefficient jumps from 0.41 to 0.61: one country was holding down the growth effect by about 50%
pop75 moves from -1.69 to -1.28; the qualitative story survives, the magnitudes do not
Nothing in summary(g) warned you; only the influence analysis did

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
Japan is influential too

g_nojapan <- lm(sr ~ pop15 + pop75 + dpi + ddpi, data = savings,
                subset = row.names(savings) != "Japan")
round(rbind(full = coef(g), no_Japan = coef(g_nojapan)), 4)

         (Intercept)   pop15   pop75    dpi   ddpi
full         28.5661 -0.4612 -1.6915 -3e-04 0.4097
no_Japan     23.9402 -0.3679 -0.9737 -5e-04 0.3347



Dropping Japan (second-highest D = 0.14) moves pop75 from -1.69 to -0.97
Two different countries, two different coefficients bent: influence is about which direction in predictor space a point sits, not just how far

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
section: What to DO about influential points
text:
What to DO about influential points

Investigate first. Is it a data error? A different population (Libya’s oil economy arguably is)? An interesting finding in itself?
Report both fits. “With and without Libya” is one honest sentence and lets readers judge; journals call this a sensitivity analysis
Never silently delete. Removing a valid observation because it disagrees with your model is choosing the story over the data

title: Week 7B: Leverage, Outliers, and Influence
text:
Deletion changes the population

If one point flips your conclusion, the honest summary is “the data do not settle this question”







Warning


Deletion changes the population you are describing. “Counties except the ones that did not fit” is not a population anyone lives in.

title: Week 6B: Fixing What the Residuals Found
text:
Where we left off

Deck A: read the plots, name the pathology
Lab A: most of you found a fan in uninsured ~ poverty
This deck: the two big fixes

Nonconstant variance: transform the outcome (sqrt, log)
Nonlinearity: add curvature or transform a predictor

Full transformation toolkit (logs both sides, Box-Cox) arrives in Week 8; today is the preview you need to patch this week’s models

title: Week 6B: Fixing What the Residuals Found
text:
What nonconstant variance actually breaks

The least squares slopes are still unbiased: the line aims at the right target
What breaks is everything that uses \sigma^2 as one number:

standard errors, so t statistics and p-values
confidence intervals
prediction intervals, worst of all: a PI that is too narrow where the data are noisy is a false promise

In public health terms: your point estimate survives; your uncertainty statements do not

title: Week 6B: Fixing What the Residuals Found
section: The remedy shelf: transform the outcome
text:
The remedy shelf: transform the outcome
Replace y with a scale where the spread is steadier:

Square root \sqrt{y}: gentle; natural for counts and skewed percentages; spread often grows with the mean, sqrt tames it
Log \log(y): stronger; for strictly positive y whose spread is proportional to its level; slopes become approximate percent differences

title: Week 6B: Fixing What the Residuals Found
text:
What a transformation costs

You now model average \sqrt{y} or average \log y, and interpretation must follow the new scale (Week 8 makes this precise)







Tip


Choose the mildest transformation that calms the residuals. You pay for strength with interpretability.

Score test: do squared residuals trend with fitted values?

Non-constant Variance Score Test 
Variance formula: ~ fitted.values 
Chisquare = 36.34807, Df = 1, p = 1.6504e-09

Non-constant Variance Score Test 
Variance formula: ~ fitted.values 
Chisquare = 2.032182, Df = 1, p = 0.154

title: Week 6B: Fixing What the Residuals Found
section: Why eyes beat tests at our sample sizes
text:
Why eyes beat tests at our sample sizes

With 3,000+ counties, a test detects departures far too small to matter: a significant ncvTest does not mean the fan is worth fixing
With 30 observations, a test misses fans you can see from across the room
The test answers “is the departure exactly zero?”; you care about “is it big enough to distort my intervals?”

title: Week 6B: Fixing What the Residuals Found
text:
Plots first, tests second

Only a plot tells you whether a departure is big enough to matter








No mechanical testing


Never run a battery of assumption tests and let p-values drive the modeling. Plots first; tests as supporting evidence; judgment always.

title: Week 6B: Fixing What the Residuals Found
text:
Nonlinearity remedies
For a curved residual plot: fix the mean function, not the variance.

Add curvature: lm(y ~ x + I(x^2)) keeps the original scale
Transform a skewed predictor: log(x) spreads out a bunched-up axis
Transforming y can also straighten a relationship, but check what it does to the spread

     xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residuals"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

title: Week 5B: When Predictions Fail
text:
The ecological fallacy, spelled out
Our slope: counties with 1 point higher poverty average 0.29 points higher uninsured rate. This is a claim about counties, not people.

It does not say a poor person is 0.29 points more likely to be uninsured; individual-level relationships can be stronger, weaker, or even reversed (the classic example: 1930 US immigrant literacy, where state-level and individual-level correlations had opposite signs)

title: Week 4B: F-tests and Comparing Models
section: Questions a single t-test cannot answer
text:
Questions a single t-test cannot answer
The t-tests this morning were one coefficient at a time. But we often need:

Do the predictors explain anything as a group? (the whole model vs nothing)
Does adding a block of terms help? (education enters as four dummy columns; “does education matter” is four coefficients at once)
Is the bigger model worth it compared to a smaller one?


All of these are F-tests: comparisons of two nested models.

title: Week 4B: F-tests and Comparing Models
text:
The overall F-test
H_0: every slope is zero (\beta_{\text{smoker}} = \beta_{\text{age}} = 0); the model is no better than predicting \bar y for everyone.

summary(fit)$fstatistic

   value    numdf    dendf 
 267.135    2.000 2085.000 



Bottom line of summary(): F = 267.1 on 2 and 2085 df, p < 2.2e-16
F: explained variation per predictor over leftover variation per residual df. Big F: far more explained than chance would give
Almost always rejected; a model that fails it is in serious trouble

title: Week 4B: F-tests and Comparing Models
text:
Nested models: does education help?
education has 5 levels, so it enters as 4 dummy columns. One question, four coefficients: a job for anova().

d_ed <- nhanes_adults |> drop_na(bp_sys, age, smoker, education)
m_small <- lm(bp_sys ~ smoker + age, data = d_ed)
m_big   <- lm(bp_sys ~ smoker + age + education, data = d_ed)
anova(m_small, m_big)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: bp_sys ~ smoker + age
Model 2: bp_sys ~ smoker + age + education
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F   Pr(>F)   
1   2085 520704                                
2   2081 516817  4    3887.1 3.9129 0.003605 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

title: Week 4B: F-tests and Comparing Models
section: One test for the whole block
text:
One test for the whole block

One p-value (0.0036) for the whole education block: education improves the model beyond smoking and age
Never read four separate dummy t-tests to decide this; they only compare each level to the reference level
Nesting requirement: the small model’s terms are a subset of the big model’s, fit to the same rows (that is why we built d_ed first)

title: Week 4B: F-tests and Comparing Models
text:
Anatomy of that ANOVA table



Column
Meaning




Res.Df
residual degrees of freedom of each model


RSS
residual sum of squares: unexplained variation


Df
4: how many coefficients the big model adds


Sum of Sq
3887: the RSS drop the new terms bought


F
(RSS drop / 4) divided by (big model RSS / its Res.Df)


Pr(>F)
how surprising that F is if the new terms are all zero

What anova() cannot do

Non-nested models: bp_sys ~ age + bmi vs bp_sys ~ age + income_mid. Neither contains the other; there is no “RSS drop from added terms” logic, so no F-test exists
Try it and R tells you so: fit to the same rows, the table comes back with Df = 0 and no F, no p-value; fit to different rows (income has missing values), anova() refuses outright

title: Week 3B: Under the Hood of Multiple Regression
section: The matrix view: a quick tour
text:
The matrix view: a quick tour
Stack the data:
\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad
X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_{11} & x_{12} \\ 1 & x_{21} & x_{22} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2} \end{pmatrix}

X is the design matrix: one row per person, one column per term (including the 1s column for the intercept)

title: Week 3B: Under the Hood of Multiple Regression
text:
Least squares in matrix form
Least squares has one formula for any number of predictors:
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathbf{y}

You will never compute this by hand; you should recognize it, because every error message and every method in this course lives in this notation

The adjusted R-squared formula
Adjusted R^2 charges a small rent per predictor:
R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{RSS/(n - p - 1)}{TSS/(n-1)}

Model selection done right comes in Week 10; today’s lesson is just: never compare models of different sizes by raw R^2

title: Week 3B: Under the Hood of Multiple Regression
text:
What adjustment cannot do

Unmeasured confounders: adjusting for age does nothing about diet, stress, income (unless measured and included)
Bad controls: adjusting for a consequence of the exposure can create bias (e.g., a medication taken because of high BP)
Measurement error: a noisy confounder is only partly adjusted for









The discipline


A regression model is an argument, not an oracle. Every variable you include (or omit) is a claim you should be able to defend out loud.

title: Week 2B: How Good Is the Line?
text:
Fitted values and residuals
Every observation splits into what the model explains and what it misses:
y_i = \underbrace{\hat y_i}_{\text{fitted}} + \underbrace{e_i}_{\text{residual}}

The residuals are our window into everything the model gets wrong (Weeks 6-7 live here)

title: Week 2B: How Good Is the Line?
section: Fitted values and residuals in R
text:
Fitted values and residuals in R

bp_aug <- bp |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(fit), resid = resid(fit))
bp_aug |> select(age, bp_sys, fitted, resid) |> head(4)

  age bp_sys   fitted      resid
1  43    103 119.8778 -16.877847
2  80     97 136.5618 -39.561816
3  34    107 115.8196  -8.819584
4  80    121 136.5618 -15.561816



Residuals always sum to zero for a least squares line with an intercept

title: Week 2B: How Good Is the Line?
text:
Decomposing variation
\underbrace{\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{TSS: total}} = \underbrace{\sum (\hat y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{explained}} + \underbrace{\sum e_i^2}_{\text{RSS: residual}}

tss <- sum((bp$bp_sys - mean(bp$bp_sys))^2)
rss <- sum(resid(fit)^2)
c(TSS = tss, RSS = rss, explained = tss - rss)

      TSS       RSS explained 
 654131.5  522138.8  131992.7

title: Week 2B: How Good Is the Line?
text:
Why the decomposition works
Add and subtract the fitted value, then square and sum:
y_i - \bar y = (\hat y_i - \bar y) + e_i, \qquad e_i = y_i - \hat y_i
\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2 = \sum (\hat y_i - \bar y)^2 + \sum e_i^2 + 2 \underbrace{\sum (\hat y_i - \bar y) e_i}_{\text{cross term}}
The identity holds exactly when the cross term is zero. That is where least squares enters: it is a property of this line, not of any line.

title: Week 2B: How Good Is the Line?
text:
The normal equations
Least squares minimizes S(b_0, b_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i)^2. Set both partial derivatives to zero:
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial S}{\partial b_0} &= -2 \sum (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i) = 0 \\[2pt]
\frac{\partial S}{\partial b_1} &= -2 \sum x_i (y_i - b_0 - b_1 x_i) = 0
\end{aligned}
At the minimizers \hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1 the parenthesis is the residual e_i, giving the normal equations \sum e_i = 0 and \sum x_i e_i = 0.

title: Week 2B: How Good Is the Line?
text:
The cross term vanishes
Since \hat y_i = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_i, split the sum:
\sum (\hat y_i - \bar y) e_i
= \hat\beta_0 \underbrace{\sum e_i}_{0}
+ \hat\beta_1 \underbrace{\sum x_i e_i}_{0}
- \bar y \underbrace{\sum e_i}_{0} = 0
Substituting back:
\underbrace{\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{TSS}} = \underbrace{\sum (\hat y_i - \bar y)^2}_{\text{explained}} + \underbrace{\sum e_i^2}_{\text{RSS}} \qquad \blacksquare

  sum_xe     = sum(bp$age * e),

title: Week 2B: How Good Is the Line?
text:
R-squared
R^2 = 1 - RSS/TSS: the fraction of the variation in y captured by the line.

c(by_hand = 1 - rss / tss,
  from_summary = summary(fit)$r.squared,
  cor_squared = cor(bp$bp_sys, bp$age)^2)

In simple regression, R^2 = r^2 exactly
Age explains about 21% of BP variation: a strong result for one variable in individual-level health data

title: Week 2B: How Good Is the Line?
text:
What is a “good” R-squared?

Physics lab: 0.99. County averages: 0.6-0.8. Individuals: 0.05-0.3
Individual outcomes are dominated by unmeasured biology and behavior; that is reality, not a failed model
A tiny R^2 can still be a precise, important association (small effects on millions of people matter in public health)








Warning


R^2 never tells you whether the model is correct, causal, or useful for prediction of individuals. It is one number, not a verdict.

Confounding

A confounder is a third variable driving both x and y
Here: national wealth buys both chocolate and research

title: Week 1B: Association Is Not Causation
text:
Association vs causation: three levels

Association: y tends to be higher when x is higher (regression can show this)
Adjusted association: …even after holding measured confounders fixed (regression can show this, if you measured the right things)
Causation: changing x would change y (needs design: randomization, natural experiments, or strong assumptions)


Regression is our tool for 1 and 2. Claiming 3 requires arguments outside the model. We will practice writing sentences that claim exactly as much as the analysis supports.

title: Week 1B: Association Is Not Causation
text:
The linear model, formally
For an outcome y and predictor x:
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n

\beta_0: intercept, the mean of y when x = 0
\beta_1: slope, the difference in mean y per one-unit difference in x
\varepsilon_i: error, everything about y_i the line does not capture


Next week: how to find the best \beta_0, \beta_1 and what “best” even means.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course Description
Regression models are one of the most important statistical techniques used in public health. This course focuses on data analysis that uses linear regression models for continuous outcomes. The first part of this course introduces simple and multiple linear regressions, principles of ordinary least square regression models, model assumptions, and inferences about model parameters. The second part of the course focuses on important practical matters, such as prediction, diagnostics, and variable selection. These two parts together provide the foundations for more advanced statistical modeling. Examples are drawn from broad areas of public health research. All the analyses will be taught and performed using R statistical software.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course Overview
This course emphasizes modern, reproducible, and active statistical practice in public health. Class sessions follow a hands-on studio rhythm: short conceptual mini-lectures alternate with guided data analyses and paired coding labs in RStudio using real-world health datasets (including NHANES, US county health metrics, and clinical trials). All computational work is done using R and Quarto. In addition, an integrated “AI Policy & Practice” component trains students to use modern AI assistants productively and defensively for exploratory coding while developing the rigorous statistical judgment required to verify, interpret, and critique quantitative outputs.

title: Homework 4
text:
Download this assignment as a .qmd file to use as your starting template.
Instructions. Complete this assignment in Quarto or R Markdown and upload both your .qmd source and the rendered .html to Brightspace. Show your code. Interpretation questions are graded on precision (adjusted for what, units, association vs causation, population), exactly as practiced in the labs. End with your AI-use statement (see Section 4).
Data. Infant mortality for 105 countries, circa the 1970s. This is a classic messy dataset: a few countries have missing mortality values, and the country names stored in the row names carry trailing spaces.

library(tidyverse)
data(infmort, package = "faraway")
inf <- infmort |>
  na.omit() |>
  rownames_to_column("country") |>
  mutate(country = str_trim(country))

Variables used below: mortality = infant deaths per 1,000 live births, income = per-capita annual income (US dollars), region = Africa, Europe, Asia, or Americas (Africa is the reference level), oil = oil exports or no oil exports. After dropping missing values, 101 countries remain.

Section 1: Do (6 points)
1.1 Show the distributions of mortality and income with histograms and a numerical summary of each. One sentence per variable on shape, mentioning where the mean sits relative to the median. (2 pts)
1.2 Fit the raw-scale model mortality ~ income and the log-log model log(mortality) ~ log(income). Report both coefficient tables and both R-squared values, and show the scatterplot on each scale with the fitted line added. One sentence on which scale the linear model describes better. (2 pts)
1.3 Extend the log-log model with the categorical predictors: log(mortality) ~ log(income) + region + oil. Report the coefficient table. (2 pts)


Section 2: Interpret (8 points; interpretation precision counts double)
2.1 Interpret the log(income) coefficient from the model in 1.3 as an elasticity, in one strong-form sentence: what percent difference in mortality is associated with a 1% difference in income, adjusted for what, in what population? (2 pts)
2.2 Interpret the regionEurope coefficient from 1.3 in one strong-form sentence, making the reference level explicit. Then convert it to a multiplicative statement about mortality using exp(). (2 pts)
2.3 Test whether region as a whole belongs in the model: compare log(mortality) ~ log(income) + oil to the full model from 1.3 with anova(). State the null hypothesis in words (how many coefficients does it constrain?), report F and the p-value, and conclude in one sentence. (2 pts)
2.4 Compute Cook’s distances for the model in 1.3 and identify the two most influential countries (they are both oil exporters). Refit the model without them and report what happens to the oil coefficient and its p-value, and to the log(income) coefficient. Two sentences on what this tells you about how fragile the oil “effect” is. (2 pts)


Section 3: Critique the AI (6 points)
A student gave this dataset to an AI assistant and asked for a write-up of the model from 1.3. The assistant replied:

“Using the 101 countries with complete data, I fit log mortality on log income, region, and oil exports. The income coefficient of -0.34 means that each additional dollar of per-capita income lowers infant mortality by 0.34 deaths per 1,000 live births. Africa does not appear in the coefficient table, which tells us the model found no region effect for African countries. The coefficient for no oil exports was -0.64; since it is negative, we conclude that exporting oil protects a country’s infants. The joint F test for region gave F = 3.2 with p = 0.03, so the region variable is only marginally useful and could reasonably be dropped. Finally, to report results on the original scale, I exponentiated the model’s predicted mean of log mortality, which gives an unbiased estimate of a country’s mean mortality rate.”

3.1 This paragraph contains at least four distinct statistical errors. Identify each one you find (quote the offending phrase), and explain in one or two sentences why it is wrong. Finding four earns full credit; a fifth earns a bonus point. (4 pts + 1 bonus)
3.2 Verify the AI’s claim about the region test by running the nested anova() comparison yourself (you did this in 2.3). Report the actual F and p-value, state whether the AI’s numbers match, and write the correct one-sentence conclusion about region. (2 pts)


Section 4: AI-use statement (required, ungraded)
One or two sentences: which AI tools you used on this assignment and for what, or “No AI tools used.” Note that Section 3 asks you to critique provided AI output; using an AI to critique the AI is permitted, but the errors you report are yours to defend.

title: Homework 2
text:
Download this assignment as a .qmd file to use as your starting template.
Instructions. Complete this assignment in Quarto or R Markdown and upload both your .qmd source and the rendered .html to Brightspace. Show your code. Data. The Stanford prostate cancer study: 97 men about to receive a radical prostatectomy, with pre-surgery measurements:

library(tidyverse)
data(prostate, package = "faraway")

Variables used below: lpsa = log of prostate-specific antigen (PSA, log ng/ml), lcavol = log cancer volume (log cm3), lweight = log prostate weight (log g), age = age (years), svi = seminal vesicle invasion (1 = yes, 0 = no). Note that the outcome and two predictors are on the log scale; interpret their coefficients in log units.

Section 1: Do (6 points)
1.1 Describe the outcome lpsa: a histogram plus a short numerical summary. Two sentences on center, spread, and shape, remembering the units are log ng/ml. (2 pts)
1.2 Fit the multiple regression of lpsa on lcavol, lweight, age, and svi. Report the coefficient table (estimates, standard errors, t values, p-values) and the residual standard error. (2 pts)
1.3 Report 95% confidence intervals for all coefficients using confint(). State which intervals exclude zero. (2 pts)


Section 2: Interpret (8 points; interpretation precision counts double)
2.1 Write the strong-form interpretation of the svi coefficient in one sentence, incorporating its confidence interval. Remember: svi is binary, the outcome is log PSA, and the sentence must state the adjustment set, the comparison being made, association wording, and the population. (2 pts)
2.2 The confidence interval for age contains zero. Write two sentences giving the correct interpretation of this interval: what range of age associations is compatible with the data, and what the interval does and does not allow you to conclude. (2 pts)
2.3 Test whether age and lweight jointly add anything beyond lcavol and svi: fit the reduced model lpsa ~ lcavol + svi and compare it to the full model with anova(). State the null hypothesis of this F test in words, report F and the p-value, and give your conclusion in one sentence. (2 pts)
2.4 Your answers to 2.2 and 2.3 may feel like they pull in opposite directions: age looks unimportant on its own, yet the pair (age, lweight) is jointly significant. In two or three sentences, reconcile this using the distinction between statistical and practical significance and the difference between individual and joint tests. Which single variable is doing the work in the joint test, and how can you tell from the coefficient table? (2 pts)


Section 3: Critique the AI (6 points)
A student pasted this dataset description into an AI assistant and asked for an inference write-up. The assistant replied:

“I fit lpsa ~ lcavol + lweight + age + svi on the 97 patients. The 95% confidence interval for age was (-0.030, 0.012); because this interval contains zero, we know the true effect of age is zero, so dropping age changes nothing. The p-value for svi was 0.002, meaning there is a 99.8% probability that seminal vesicle invasion affects PSA. Comparing lpsa ~ lcavol + svi against the full model, anova() gave F = 6.11 with p = 0.003, which proves that age and lweight each individually improve the model. Also, lcavol’s t statistic of 7.43 is more than double svi’s 3.17, so cancer volume has more than twice as large an effect on PSA as seminal vesicle invasion. Age itself was clearly irrelevant (p = 0.52).”

3.1 This paragraph contains at least four distinct statistical errors. Identify each one you find (quote the offending phrase), and explain in one or two sentences why it is wrong. Finding four earns full credit; a fifth earns a bonus point. (4 pts + 1 bonus)
3.2 Verify the AI’s inference claims about age by fitting the models yourself. Report the actual p-value for age in the full model and the actual F and p-value from the nested anova() comparison, state which of the AI’s numbers do not match, and write the correct one-sentence conclusion about what the joint test does and does not show. (2 pts)

title: Sample Warm-Up Quiz 1
text:
Answer key
Do all ten first.
Q1. B. (three jobs a model can do) The model is being used to anticipate a future value from a new x, which is prediction. Description would be summarizing the relationship in past data; explanation would be claiming that changing the temperature changes admissions.
Q2. D. (regression to the mean) Selection on an extreme outcome guarantees that luck contributed to it, so the next measurement drifts back toward the athlete’s true average. This is the same mechanism as the clinic that re-measures its highest-BP patients, and it is why single-arm before-after studies are so misleading.
Q3. C. (confounding) A confounder drives both variables. B describes an outlier and D describes the error term or residual: correct vocabulary, wrong object.
Q4. B. (association and causation) Adjustment moves you from level 1 to level 2 of the hierarchy, and no further. The honest sentence names the variables you adjusted for and admits that unmeasured confounding remains possible. C is the most common overreach in write-ups.
Q5. D. (the least squares criterion) A line that misses badly in both directions can still have residuals summing to zero. In fact every least squares line with an intercept has \sum e_i = 0, so this criterion cannot distinguish good lines from bad ones. B describes an argument against squaring, not against summing.
Q6. C. (computing the slope) -0.30 \times 6.0 / 1.5 = -1.20. D is r \cdot s_y / s_x with the standard deviations swapped in your head, and B is r \cdot s_y without dividing. Keep the units attached and the arithmetic checks itself: kg/m^2 divided by hours gives kg/m^2 per hour.
Q7. A. (interpreting the slope) Number, units, direction, “on average”, and a comparison between people. B is causal, which this design cannot support. D confuses a slope in the original units with a percentage change.
Q8. A. (the intercept) The intercept is always the model’s average y when x = 0. What makes it interpretable here is that x = 0 is a real, observed group: adults who do no vigorous exercise. Contrast this with a model of BP on age, where x = 0 means newborns and lies far outside the data, so the intercept is only a mathematical anchor. C describes where the line crosses the x-axis, which is a different quantity, and D is the slope.
Q9. A. (r-squared) Small R^2 values are normal for individual-level health outcomes, where most variation comes from biology and behavior you did not measure. A small R^2 does not make an association unimportant, and it does not make the model wrong.
Q10. B. (changing the measurements) Shifting every y by a constant slides the whole cloud of points up without tilting it. Formally, \hat\beta_1 depends on y only through y_i - \bar y, and adding 5 to every y_i also adds 5 to \bar y, so the deviations and the slope are untouched. The intercept then moves with the mean: \hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x gains exactly 5. D is tempting if you remember that “constants cancel” in the slope, but the intercept is precisely where the constant does not cancel.

title: Sample Warm-Up Quiz 1
text:
One more thing worth knowing
This did not fit as a question, but it is the mistake that costs the most marks on the interpretation questions, so it is worth thirty seconds now.
Compare these two sentences about a slope of -0.32 for sleep hours:

Adults who sleep one hour more have, on average, 0.32 kg/m^2 lower BMI.


Sleeping one more hour lowers BMI by 0.32 kg/m^2.

The first compares different people at one moment, which is what cross-sectional data contains. The second describes what happens inside one person over time, which the data never observed. The numbers are identical and the claims are not.
When you write an interpretation, check that it contains four things: the number, the units, the direction, and a phrase such as “on average” or “is associated with”. If the sentence would still make sense as an instruction to a patient, it is probably too strong.

title: Sample Warm-Up Quiz 1
section: Systematic changes to x or y
text:
Systematic changes to x or y
Question 10 is one case of a pattern worth knowing in general. Everything below follows from the two formulas you already have,
\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2},
\qquad \hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x.








Change to the data
New slope
New intercept




Add a to every x_i
\hat\beta_1
\hat\beta_0 - a\hat\beta_1


Add b to every y_i
\hat\beta_1
\hat\beta_0 + b


Multiply every x_i by c
\hat\beta_1 / c
\hat\beta_0


Multiply every y_i by d
d\,\hat\beta_1
d\,\hat\beta_0



Two things to take from the table. Shifting either variable never changes the slope, because the slope is built from deviations around the mean and a shift moves the mean by the same amount. Rescaling changes the slope by exactly the factor needed to keep the fitted line in the same place: measuring age in decades rather than years divides x by 10, so the slope is multiplied by 10 and describes a decade instead of a year.
In every row the fitted line is the same line, drawn on relabelled axes, so the residuals are unchanged up to the same rescaling and R^2 does not move at all. Only the description changes, which is why units belong in every interpretation you write.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text: This course treats AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, and similar) as standard tools of modern statistical practice. You will learn to use them effectively and critically, while developing the solid statistical foundation to evaluate and explain models without them.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text:
Why this policy
In professional biostatistics and public health data science, computing models is fast, but judgment, interpretation in context, and diagnostic scrutiny are what protect against false conclusions.
AI tools are prone to subtle statistical errors: 1. Conflating statistical association with causal effects. 2. Fabricating interpretations of adjusted regression coefficients that ignore confounding structures. 3. Overlooking severe residual non-linearity or influential outliers. 4. Hallucinating package syntax, citations, or data definitions.
Banning AI tools would fail to prepare you for modern practice; relying on them blindly would leave you unable to catch their errors. This course trains you to direct AI tools purposefully, verify their mathematical and contextual accuracy, and take full ownership of your statistical work.

title: AI Policy: The Three Zones
text:
Requirements & Ethics

Free-tier tools are sufficient: All coursework can be completed with free-tier AI assistants; no paid subscriptions are required or expected.
Ownership: “The AI told me to” is never an acceptable defense for an erroneous model, an incorrect interpretation, or broken code.
Integrity: Submitting AI-generated analyses you cannot explain, using AI during quizzes or exams, or omitting required disclosures constitutes an academic integrity violation.

title: AI Ground Rules
text: AI assistants are part of how statistics gets done now. Banning them would teach you nothing about using them well, and “using them well” is a skill your employers will expect. So here is the deal.

title: AI Ground Rules
text:
The three rules
1. Use it. On homework and the project you may use AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, or similar) to learn concepts, debug code, explore approaches, and improve writing. Some homework problems will hand you AI output and require you to critique it.
2. Disclose it. Every homework and project submission ends with a one- or two-sentence AI-use statement. Examples:

“I used Claude to debug a ggplot error in Q2 and to suggest wording for my Q4 interpretation, which I revised.”


“No AI tools used.”

Honest disclosure is never penalized. Missing or false disclosure is an academic integrity violation.
3. Own it. You are responsible for every word and number you submit. “The AI said so” does not excuse a wrong answer, an invented reference, or code you cannot explain. I may ask you to walk me through any part of your submission, and the biweekly quizzes and final exam (both in class, no AI) check that the understanding is actually yours.

text:
What good use looks like

“Explain why my residual plot fans out and what that violates” then reading the cited textbook section to confirm
Pasting an error message and asking for the bug, then understanding the fix before moving on
Drafting an interpretation yourself, asking AI to critique it, keeping your own voice

Submitting code you cannot explain. It shows immediately when I ask.

Why the quizzes and exam are AI-free
Not distrust; calibration. You need regular, honest evidence of what you can do unaided, and so do I. Think of AI-free checkpoints as the treadmill stress test and AI-assisted work as daily life with your fitness tracker on.

title: Homework 1
text:
Download this assignment as a .qmd file to use as your starting template.
Instructions. Complete this assignment in Quarto or R Markdown and upload both your .qmd source and the rendered .html to Brightspace. Show your code. Interpretation questions are graded on precision (adjusted for what, units, association vs causation, population), exactly as practiced in Labs 2 and 3. End with your AI-use statement (see Section 4).
Data. The Baystate Medical Center birth weight study (Springfield, MA, 1986), 189 births:

library(tidyverse)
data(birthwt, package = "MASS")
births <- birthwt |>
  mutate(smoke = factor(smoke, labels = c("Non-smoker", "Smoker")))

Variables used below: bwt = birth weight (grams), lwt = mother’s pre-pregnancy weight (pounds), age = mother’s age (years), smoke = smoking during pregnancy.

Section 1: Do (6 points)
1.1 Describe the outcome bwt: a histogram plus a short numerical summary. Two sentences on center, spread, and shape, with units. (2 pts)
1.2 Fit the simple linear regression of bwt on lwt. Report the fitted equation and add the fitted line to a scatterplot (use your coefficients with geom_abline, not geom_smooth). (2 pts)
1.3 Using arithmetic on your coefficients, give the model’s expected birth weight for mothers weighing 120 and 200 pounds. State which prediction you trust more, and why, referring to the data. (2 pts)


Section 2: Interpret (8 points; interpretation precision counts double)
2.1 Interpret the slope from 1.2 in one strong-form sentence. (2 pts)
2.2 The R-squared of this model is about 0.03. A journalist concludes the model is “useless.” Give a two-sentence rebuttal that concedes what the model cannot do and states what the slope estimate still offers. (2 pts)
2.3 Fit bwt ~ smoke, then bwt ~ smoke + lwt. Report the smoking coefficient from both. Does adjusting for mother’s weight change the smoking association much here? Using the group means of lwt by smoking status, explain in one sentence why the adjustment behaves the way it does. (2 pts)
2.4 Write the strong-form interpretation of the smoking coefficient in the adjusted model, then a second sentence stating clearly one reason this is not an estimate of the causal effect of smoking cessation. (2 pts)


Section 3: Critique the AI (6 points)
A student pasted this dataset description into an AI assistant and asked for an analysis. The assistant replied:

“I fit a regression of birth weight on mother’s age and found a slope of 12.4 grams per year. Since the intercept is 2656 grams, a newborn whose mother is age zero would weigh 2656 grams. The p-value for age was 0.19, which proves that mother’s age has no effect on birth weight. Because heavier mothers tend to be older, I also recommend removing lwt from any model that includes age, since two correlated predictors cannot be used together in linear regression. Overall, since this regression is based on a proper hospital sample, the slope of 12.4 tells us how much a mother’s baby will gain if she delays pregnancy by one year.”

3.1 This paragraph contains at least four distinct statistical errors. Identify each one you find (quote the offending phrase), and explain in one or two sentences why it is wrong. Finding four earns full credit; a fifth earns a bonus point. (4 pts + 1 bonus)
3.2 Verify one of the AI’s numerical claims by fitting bwt ~ age yourself. Report whether the slope and intercept match, and write the correct one-sentence conclusion about the age association that the data actually support. (2 pts)


Section 4: AI-use statement (required, ungraded)
One or two sentences: which AI tools you used on this assignment and for what, or “No AI tools used.” Note that Section 3 asks you to critique provided AI output; using an AI to critique the AI is permitted, but the errors you report are yours to defend.

title: Homework 3
text:

Instructions. Complete this assignment in Quarto or R Markdown and upload both your .qmd source and the rendered .html to Brightspace. Show your code. Data. A British survey of 47 teenagers on gambling and its covariates:

data(teengamb, package = "faraway")

Variables used below: gamble = expenditure on gambling (pounds per year), income = income (pounds per week), sex = 0 for male, 1 for female, status = socioeconomic status score of parents. Note that sex is coded numerically; you may use it as is or convert it to a labeled factor.

Section 1: Do (6 points)
1.1 Fit the multiple regression of gamble on income, sex, and status. Report the coefficient table and R-squared. (2 pts)
1.2 For two profiles, (a) a male with income 5 and status 50, and (b) a female with income 5 and status 50, compute both the 95% confidence interval for the mean response and the 95% prediction interval for a new individual, using predict() with interval = "confidence" and interval = "prediction". Present the four intervals in a small table. (2 pts)
1.3 Make the residuals-versus-fitted plot for your model (residuals on the y axis, fitted values on the x axis, with a horizontal line at zero). (2 pts)


Section 2: Interpret (8 points; interpretation precision counts double)
2.1 Using the male profile from 1.2, explain in two sentences, in plain words a public health colleague could follow, what the confidence interval estimates and what the prediction interval estimates, and why the prediction interval is so much wider. (2 pts)
2.2 Describe what you see in the residual plot from 1.3. Name the specific assumption violations the plot shows (there are at least two: consider the spread of the residuals across fitted values, and their symmetry), and point to the features of the plot that reveal them. (2 pts)
2.3 Given your diagnosis in 2.2, would you trust the 95% prediction intervals from 1.2 to actually cover new observations 95% of the time? Explain in two sentences which specific violation undermines the PI and how (think about what the PI formula assumes about the error distribution). (2 pts)
2.4 Propose a remedy: refit the model with sqrt(gamble) as the outcome (or log(gamble + 1) if you prefer), remake the residual plot, and state in two sentences whether the problems improved and what interpretability price you paid for the fix. (2 pts)

A student gave this dataset to an AI assistant and asked for a prediction write-up. The assistant replied:

“The model gamble ~ income + sex + status explains 61% of the variation in gambling expenditure. For a male teenager with income 5 and status 50, the 95% confidence interval is (21.4, 39.0) pounds, so we can be 95% sure that this individual will spend between 21 and 39 pounds per year on gambling. Since the model fits well, the regression assumptions are clearly satisfied and residual plots are unnecessary. The model is also useful well beyond the survey: a teenager earning 20 pounds per week is predicted to spend 104 pounds per year, an especially reliable prediction because it comes directly from the fitted equation. Finally, for a female with income 1 and status 60 the model predicts -15.4 pounds, meaning she would earn about 15 pounds per year from gambling.”

Rubric (15 pts):

Introduction (2): question, motivation, data source described
Methods (3): models stated precisely, choices justified (transformations, included variables), inference approach described
Results (6): estimation with interpretation (2), inference (1), diagnostics with consequences addressed (2), model comparison/selection (1)
Discussion (2): findings in context, limitations including confounding
Writing quality and reproducibility (2): report reads cleanly; code in appendix reruns from the raw data

title: Course Project
text:
Picking a dataset
Any public dataset with a continuous outcome and enough observations (n of 200+ recommended) works. Good starting points:

County Health Rankings: county-level health outcomes and factors (countyhealthrankings.org)
NHANES (raw waves, different variables than class): CDC NHANES
BRFSS: state/individual behavioral risk factors (CDC BRFSS)
CDC PLACES: census-tract health estimates (CDC PLACES)
Gapminder / WHO Global Health Observatory: country-level indicators (who.int/data/gho)
EPA Air Quality System: pollution measurements (epa.gov/outdoor-air-quality-data)
NYC Open Data: restaurant inspections, health surveys, vital statistics (opendata.cityofnewyork.us)
IPUMS Health Surveys: harmonized NHIS/MEPS microdata (healthsurveys.ipums.org)
Global Burden of Disease: country-year disease burden (ghdx.healthdata.org)
Tidy Tuesday archives: many curated health-adjacent sets (github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday)

Avoid: time series as your only structure (we do not cover it), binary outcomes (that is Regression II: logistic), and datasets so clean they teach you nothing. A little messiness is a feature; document what you did about it.

What is a regression question?
All of these are regression questions:

How much does systolic blood pressure rise per decade of age, and does the rate differ between smokers and non-smokers?
Which county characteristics best predict premature death rates, and how well?
After adjusting for age and income, is sleep duration associated with BMI?


Common structure: a continuous outcome y, one or more predictors x, and a question about the relationship.

title: Week 1A: What Regression Is For
section: Three jobs a regression model can do
text:
Three jobs a regression model can do

Description: summarize how y varies with x in these data
Prediction: given a new x, what y should we expect, and how sure are we?
Explanation: what happens to y if x changes? (causal, the hardest)








Warning


Same lm() output, three very different claims. Most regression disasters come from doing job 1 and announcing job 3.

The “sophomore slump” and magazine-cover jinx

title: Week 2A: Least Squares
text:
This week’s question
How much does systolic blood pressure differ with age among US adults?

Data: bp, the NHANES adults with both bp_sys and age recorded
Outcome y: systolic BP (mmHg); predictor x: age (years)
First step, always: look at the scatterplot


bp_cloud <- ggplot(bp, aes(age, bp_sys)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)")

title: Week 2A: Least Squares
text:
Systolic BP by age










A cloud, not a line
Our job: choose a trend line by a defensible rule

title: Week 2A: Least Squares
text:
The simple linear regression model
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i

y_i: systolic BP of person i; x_i: their age
\beta_0, \beta_1: unknown parameters describing the population
\varepsilon_i: error term, everything else that moves BP (genes, diet, measurement error)


We never see \beta_0, \beta_1. We compute estimates \hat\beta_0,
\hat\beta_1 from data, and the hat matters.

title: Week 2A: Least Squares
text:
Which line is “best”?
Residual for any candidate line: e_i = y_i - (\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_i)

Why not minimize \sum e_i? Positive and negative misses cancel; a terrible line can have sum zero
Why not \sum |e_i|? Legitimate (and used!), but no calculus-friendly closed form
Least squares: minimize \sum e_i^2: penalizes big misses heavily, and the solution is exact and unique

title: Week 2A: Least Squares
text:
The least squares solution
Minimizing \sum_i (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 over (\beta_0, \beta_1) gives:
\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2} = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x}, \qquad \hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x

Slope: correlation rescaled by the ratio of standard deviations
Intercept: forces the line through (\bar x, \bar y)



c(slope_by_hand = with(bp, cor(age, bp_sys) * sd(bp_sys) / sd(age)),
  slope_from_lm = unname(coef(lm(bp_sys ~ age, data = bp))[2]))

title: Week 3A: More Than One Predictor
text:
The multiple regression model
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \varepsilon_i

Same least squares idea: choose all the \hat\beta_j at once to minimize \sum e_i^2
Geometrically: fitting a plane (or hyperplane) instead of a line
R syntax just adds terms: lm(bp_sys ~ smoker + age)

title: Week 3A: More Than One Predictor
text:
Adjusting for age

coef(lm(bp_sys ~ smoker, data = d))

 (Intercept) smokerSmoker 
  120.185751     3.935734 

coef(lm(bp_sys ~ smoker + age, data = d))

 (Intercept) smokerSmoker          age 
 100.2188301    1.6833807    0.4413965 



Unadjusted: +3.9 mmHg for smokers
Age-adjusted: +1.7 mmHg: more than half of the gap was age, not smoke
This one move (and knowing when to trust it) is most of applied regression in public health

title: Week 3A: More Than One Predictor
section: How to read an adjusted coefficient
text:
How to read an adjusted coefficient
For bp_sys ~ smoker + age, the smoker coefficient means:

Comparing two adults of the same age, the smoker averages 1.7 mmHg higher systolic BP.


“Holding age fixed” or “adjusting for age” or “comparing like with like on age”
It does not say what happens if a person quits smoking (still observational!)
It does not adjust for anything left out of the model (diet, income, …)

title: Week 3A: More Than One Predictor
text:
Think-pair-share (3 min)
In our data, bp_sys ~ smoker + age gives a smoker coefficient of +1.7.

Someone claims: “so quitting would lower a smoker’s BP by 1.7 mmHg.” Name two distinct reasons this claim overreaches.
What variable would you add next, and what do you predict happens to the smoking coefficient?

title: Week 3A: More Than One Predictor
section: Continuous predictors adjust the same way
text:
Continuous predictors adjust the same way

coef(lm(bp_sys ~ age + bmi, data = d))

(Intercept)         age         bmi 
 93.0870579   0.4436233   0.2693857 



Age slope barely moves (0.45 to 0.44): age and BMI are nearly unrelated in adults, so they explain different parts of BP
BMI: comparing same-age adults, each extra BMI unit is associated with +0.27 mmHg
When predictors are correlated, coefficients shift on adjustment; when they are not, they barely move. Watching what moves is diagnostic gold

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
text:
This week’s question
Is the age-adjusted smoking association real, or noise?
Last week you found it:

coef(lm(bp_sys ~ smoker + age, data = d))

 (Intercept) smokerSmoker          age 
 100.0804162    1.6917075    0.4442294 



Comparing same-age adults, smokers average about 1.7 mmHg higher systolic BP
But 1.7 is a number computed from one sample of 2088 people
A different sample would give a different number. How different?

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
section: The wobble, now for a coefficient
text:
The wobble, now for a coefficient
Week 2 showed the fitted line wobbling across samples. Same idea, tracking one coefficient: resample our data 500 times, refit, keep the smoker coefficient.

set.seed(2026)
boots <- map_dbl(1:500, \(k) {
  coef(lm(bp_sys ~ smoker + age,
          data = slice_sample(d, n = nrow(d), replace = TRUE)))["smokerSmoker"]
})
ggplot(tibble(b = boots), aes(b)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Smoker coefficient across resamples", y = "Count")

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
section: The sampling distribution of the coefficient
text:
The sampling distribution of the coefficient










A sampling distribution: some resamples land near 0
Inference: describe this spread without resampling

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
text:
The standard error
Theory gives us the spread of that histogram from a single sample:

summary(fit)$coefficients

                Estimate Std. Error   t value      Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  100.0804162 1.00900547 99.187189  0.000000e+00
smokerSmoker   1.6917075 0.70577605  2.396947  1.661988e-02
age            0.4442294 0.01981146 22.422852 6.134813e-100



Std. Error estimates the standard deviation of \hat\beta_j across hypothetical repeated samples: here about 0.71 mmHg for the smoker coefficient
Small SE: the estimate would barely move in a new sample. Large SE: do not get attached to the point estimate

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
text:
The t-test for one coefficient
To ask “could this association be pure noise?”, test
H_0: \beta_{\text{smoker}} = 0 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_1: \beta_{\text{smoker}} \ne 0,
\qquad t = \frac{\hat\beta_j - 0}{\widehat{SE}(\hat\beta_j)}

Here t = 1.69 / 0.71 \approx 2.40: 2.4 SEs away from zero
Under H_0, t has a t-distribution with n - p - 1 = 2088 - 3
= 2085 df (essentially normal at this size)
p-value: the probability, if \beta_j = 0, of a t at least this far from zero

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
text:
Reading summary() precisely

summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = bp_sys ~ smoker + age, data = d)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-51.398  -9.634  -1.075   8.482  97.016 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  100.08042    1.00901  99.187   <2e-16 ***
smokerSmoker   1.69171    0.70578   2.397   0.0166 *  
age            0.44423    0.01981  22.423   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 15.8 on 2085 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.204, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2032 
F-statistic: 267.1 on 2 and 2085 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
section: What the p-value is, and is not
text:
What the p-value is, and is not
Smoker row: estimate 1.69, SE 0.71, t = 2.40, p = 0.017. If smoking and BP were unrelated after age adjustment, a gap this large would arise in about 1.7% of samples. p = 0.017 does not mean:

a 1.7% chance that H_0 is true (it is a statement about data given H_0, not about H_0 given data)
the association is large or clinically important (that is the estimate’s job)
the association is causal (nothing about the design changed)

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
text:
Each t-test is conditional







One test, one row


Each t-test in the table tests one coefficient with everything else already in the model. The smoker p-value asks whether smoking adds anything beyond age, not whether smoking matters in isolation.





Add or drop other predictors and a row’s p-value can change

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
section: Confidence intervals: the estimate with honest error bars
text:
Confidence intervals: the estimate with honest error bars

confint(fit)

                  2.5 %      97.5 %
(Intercept)  98.1016531 102.0591792
smokerSmoker  0.3076084   3.0758066
age           0.4053771   0.4830817



Recipe: \hat\beta_j \pm t^* \cdot \widehat{SE}(\hat\beta_j), with t^*
\approx 1.96 at this sample size
Age-adjusted smoking gap: 0.31 to 3.08 mmHg. The interval excludes 0, which is exactly why p < 0.05
The interval says more than the p-value: the data are consistent with a trivial gap (0.3) and with a modest one (3), and rule out huge ones

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
section: What a 95% CI does and does not mean
text:
What a 95% CI does and does not mean

Does mean: the procedure captures the true coefficient in 95% of repeated samples. Our interval is one draw from that procedure
Does not mean: there is a 95% probability that \beta is in (0.31, 3.08). After computing it, the interval either contains \beta or it does not; the 95% describes the method’s long-run track record
Does not mean: 95% of smokers have BP elevations in this range (it is about the average gap, not individuals)

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
text:
Think-pair-share (3 min)
The age row reads: estimate 0.444, 95% CI (0.405, 0.483), p < 2e-16.

Your teammate says “we are 95% sure the true age coefficient is between 0.405 and 0.483.” Is that the exact meaning? What is the careful version?
Another teammate says “age has a smaller p-value than smoking, so age matters more for BP.” Name what is wrong with that comparison.
Write the one-sentence report of the age result you would actually publish.

title: Week 4A: From Estimate to Inference
section: The strong-form sentence, now with a CI
text:
The strong-form sentence, now with a CI
Week 3’s strong form plus uncertainty is the full reporting standard:

Adjusting for age, US adults who have smoked 100+ cigarettes average 1.7 mmHg higher systolic blood pressure than never-smokers (95% CI 0.3 to 3.1 mmHg, p = 0.017) in NHANES 2011-2012. This is an association, not an estimate of the effect of smoking or quitting.


Adjustment set, units, population, association language: all still there
New ingredients: the interval and the p-value, stated with the estimate, never instead of it

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
section: Two different jobs for the same lm()
text:
Two different jobs for the same lm()
Weeks 3-4: explanation. Which predictors matter, how big is the adjusted association, is it real?
This week: prediction. Given a county’s characteristics, what uninsured rate should we expect, and how sure are we?

Same fitted model, different questions, different loyalties
Explanation obsesses over one coefficient’s meaning; prediction obsesses over \hat y and its error bars
A model can be excellent at one job and poor at the other

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
text:
This week’s question
How well can we predict a county’s uninsured rate, and how sure are we?
New dataset, new scale: county_health (ACS 2019, via the usdata package).

ch |> select(state, name, uninsured, poverty, unemployment, median_age) |>
  slice_sample(n = 4, replace = FALSE)

# A tibble: 4 × 6
  state       name            uninsured poverty unemployment median_age
  <chr>       <chr>               <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Minnesota   Olmsted County        3.9     8.4          2.6       37.2
2 Michigan    Houghton County       7      20.2          5.1       33  
3 Mississippi Pike County          13.8    33            4.6       37.2
4 Ohio        Lake County           4.7     8.1          3.8       43.8

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
text:
The outcome and the unit

Outcome: uninsured = % of residents without health insurance, a system-level public health outcome
One row = one county, not one person. Everything is a county average or percentage; keep that in mind all day (it bites in lecture B)

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
text:
Data honesty first

c(counties = nrow(county_health), complete = nrow(ch))

counties complete 
    3142     1266 

summary(ch$uninsured)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  1.800   5.700   8.450   9.106  11.500  36.500 



The 2019 ACS one-year estimates exist only for larger counties, so our modeling set of 1,266 counties over-represents populous ones (median population about 92,000 vs 13,000 among the dropped)
Uninsured rates run from about 2% to 36%: massive policy-relevant variation

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
section: The model, and predict() with newdata
text:
The model, and predict() with newdata

m <- lm(uninsured ~ poverty + unemployment + median_age, data = ch)
coef(m)

 (Intercept)      poverty unemployment   median_age 
   8.6798723    0.2861535    0.0349146   -0.1061795 

new_county <- tibble(poverty = 15, unemployment = 5, median_age = 40)
predict(m, newdata = new_county)

       1 
8.899566 



predict() plugs the new predictor values into the fitted equation: expected uninsured rate about 8.9% for this profile
newdata must contain every predictor, with the same names
A point prediction with no error bars is a half-answer. There are two very different full answers…

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
text:
Two questions, two intervals
Question 1 (mean response): among all counties with poverty 15%, unemployment 5%, median age 40, what is the average uninsured rate?
Question 2 (single county): this particular new county has that profile. What is its uninsured rate?

Q1 needs a confidence interval: uncertainty about where the regression surface sits (only estimation wobble in \hat\beta)
Q2 needs a prediction interval: surface wobble plus the county-to-county scatter around the surface (\sigma, estimated at 3.9 points)

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
text:
Both, from the same function

predict(m, newdata = new_county, interval = "confidence")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 8.899566 8.678986 9.120147

predict(m, newdata = new_county, interval = "prediction")

       fit      lwr      upr
1 8.899566 1.218996 16.58014



CI: the average uninsured rate for counties like this is between 8.7 and 9.1%. Tight, because n = 1,266 pins down the surface well
PI: this one county could plausibly be anywhere from about 1 to 17%. Wide, because counties with identical poverty, unemployment, and age still differ enormously (state policy, immigration, labor markets…)

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
section: Why the PI is always wider
text:
Why the PI is always wider

Conceptually: SE_{CI}^2 reflects \widehat{Var}(\hat y) alone, while SE_{PI}^2 = \widehat{Var}(\hat y) + \hat\sigma^2. The PI is always wider
More data shrinks the CI toward zero width; the PI can never shrink below the residual scatter

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
text:
Seeing both bands: the code
Both intervals on a grid of poverty values, from a one-predictor model:

m1 <- lm(uninsured ~ poverty, data = ch)
grid <- tibble(poverty = seq(min(ch$poverty), max(ch$poverty), length.out = 200))
bands <- bind_cols(
  grid,
  as_tibble(predict(m1, grid, interval = "confidence")) |>
    rename(ci_lo = lwr, ci_hi = upr),
  as_tibble(predict(m1, grid, interval = "prediction")) |>
    select(pi_lo = lwr, pi_hi = upr)
)



Code
bands_plot <- ggplot(ch, aes(poverty, uninsured)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(data = bands, aes(y = fit, ymin = pi_lo, ymax = pi_hi),
              fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(data = bands, aes(y = fit, ymin = ci_lo, ymax = ci_hi),
              fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = bands, aes(y = fit), color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Poverty rate (%)", y = "Uninsured (%)")

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
text:
Seeing both bands










Inner: CI for the mean. Outer: PI (covers about 95%)
Both flare at the edges, where data are thin

title: Week 5A: Prediction and Its Uncertainty
text:
Think-pair-share (3 min)
A state health office asks: “Counties with 20% poverty: what uninsured rate should we budget for?”

Is that a mean-response question or a single-county question? Could it be either, depending on what “budget for” means?
At poverty 20%, the model says fit 10.5, CI (10.3, 10.8), PI (2.8, 18.3). Write the one-sentence answer for each reading of the question.
Which interval would you give a county executive planning one county’s clinic capacity, and why?

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text:
This week’s question
Your model makes assumptions; the residuals show where it breaks them.

Every lm() you have fit so far came with fine print you signed without reading
Weeks 4-5 (t tests, CIs, prediction intervals) all lean on that fine print
This week and next: how to read the fine print, and how to catch the model breaking it
The informants are the residuals e_i = y_i - \hat y_i: everything the model got wrong, one number per observation

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text:
The fine print: the model
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \varepsilon_i

The standard assumptions are all about the errors \varepsilon_i
We never see \varepsilon_i. We see the residuals e_i, which estimate them

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
section: The fine print: four assumptions on the errors
text:
The fine print: four assumptions on the errors

Mean zero given the predictors: the linear form is right; nothing systematic is left over
Constant variance: the scatter around the line is the same everywhere (\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2)
Independence: one observation’s error tells you nothing about another’s
Normality: the errors follow a normal distribution

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
section: Rank them: not all violations are equal
text:
Rank them: not all violations are equal



Rank
Assumption
If violated




1
Mean zero (linearity)
Estimates aim at the wrong target


2
Constant variance
Slopes fine; SEs, CIs, PIs wrong


3
Independence
SEs can be badly off


4
Normality
Matters least: PIs, small n (Week 7)

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text:
Using the ranking

The ranking guides your energy: chase curvature first, fans second
Independence is mostly a design question (repeated measures? clustered? time-ordered?), not a plot question

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
section: Why residuals vs fitted is the workhorse
text:
Why residuals vs fitted is the workhorse

Plot e_i (vertical) against \hat y_i (horizontal)
If the model is right, residuals are what is left after removing all structure: the plot should be a boring, structureless blob centered at zero
Anything visible (a curve, a fan, a stray point) is structure the model missed
One plot works for any number of predictors, because \hat y_i compresses them all onto one axis

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
section: The workhorse on a familiar model
text:
The workhorse on a familiar model







The null plot


Train your eyes on what “nothing” looks like. Diagnosing is comparing your plot to boring.





plot(fitted(fit_bp), resid(fit_bp),
     xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "bp_sys ~ age (NHANES adults)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
section: The workhorse on a familiar model
text:
The workhorse on a familiar model










Centered at zero across the range: no obvious curve
Slightly more spread at high fitted values: keep that for deck B

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text:
A gallery with known answers
Four simulated datasets, same straight-line model lm(y ~ x) fit to each. I know the truth because I wrote the code. Diagnose each panel.


Code
set.seed(601)
n <- 120
x <- runif(n, 0, 10)
gallery <- bind_rows(
  tibble(panel = "A", x = x, y = 2 + 0.7 * x + rnorm(n, sd = 0.25 * x)),
  tibble(panel = "B", x = x, y = 2 + 0.7 * x + rnorm(n, sd = 1.2)),
  tibble(panel = "C", x = x, y = 2 + 0.7 * x + c(rnorm(n - 1, sd = 1.2), 9)),
  tibble(panel = "D", x = x,
         y = 2 + 0.7 * x - 0.18 * (x - 5)^2 + rnorm(n, sd = 1.2))
)
gallery_resid <- gallery |>
  group_by(panel) |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(lm(y ~ x)), resid = resid(lm(y ~ x))) |>
  ungroup()
gallery_plot <- ggplot(gallery_resid, aes(fitted, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text: The gallery

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text:
Gallery, answered: A and B

A: fan. Errors were generated with sd = 0.25 * x: spread grows with the fitted value. Nonconstant variance
B: nothing. Honest constant-variance noise. This is what healthy looks like: hold onto it

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text:
Gallery, answered: C and D

C: one outlier. All errors normal except one observation pushed up by 9 (about 7 standard deviations). One point, far from the band
D: curve. The truth includes -0.18(x-5)^2; the straight line misses systematically, so residuals arc: positive, negative, positive








Warning


Real plots whisper; simulations shout. The lab drills you on the same four shapes so you recognize the whisper.

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text:
Pattern, problem, consequence








You see
It suggests
What it costs you




Curve or arc
Wrong mean function (nonlinearity)
Biased estimates; wrong story


Fan or funnel
Nonconstant variance
Wrong SEs, CIs, p-values, PIs


Isolated stray point
Outlier or data error
Can drag the whole fit (Week 7)


Boring blob
Nothing detectable
Carry on




“No visible problem” only rules out problems big enough to see

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text:
Residuals vs individual predictors
\hat y compresses all predictors onto one axis, which can hide which predictor is at fault. Plot residuals against each predictor too.


Code
set.seed(602)
m <- 200
x1 <- runif(m, 0, 10)
x2 <- runif(m, -3, 3)
y <- 1 + x1 + x2^2 + rnorm(m)
fit2 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2)
sim2 <- tibble(x1, x2, resid = resid(fit2)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(x1, x2), names_to = "predictor", values_to = "value")
sim2_plot <- ggplot(sim2, aes(value, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~predictor, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Predictor value", y = "Residuals")

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text:
Residuals vs individual predictors










Truth: y = 1 + x_1 + x_2^2 + \varepsilon. Fine vs x_1; a parabola vs x_2
Routine: residuals vs fitted first, then vs each predictor

title: Week 6A: Reading the Residuals
text:
Think-pair-share (2 min)
A classmate fits uninsured ~ poverty on county data and finds a clear fan: residual spread grows with fitted values.

Which assumption is in question?
Is the estimated slope biased because of this?
Which parts of last week’s output should they distrust?


Fan means assumption 2, not assumption 1: the slope is still an unbiased estimate of the linear association, but its SE, the CIs, and especially the prediction intervals are built on a variance that is not one number.

title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
text:
This week’s question
One county (or country) can move your whole model.

Last week: linearity and constant variance, the loud assumptions
Today, deck A: the two quieter assumptions

Normality of the errors: how to check it, when it matters
Independence: checked with your study design, not a plot

Deck B: single observations that quietly run the show: leverage, outliers, influence

title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
text:
The Q-Q plot
To check normality, compare the sorted residuals to where sorted values should fall if they were normal.

Plot the i-th smallest residual against the normal quantile \Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{i}{n+1}\right)
If residuals are normal: points hug a straight line
Departures have signatures: tails that peel off, curves that bend one way

title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
section: The Q-Q plot for our BP model
text:
The Q-Q plot for our BP model

qqnorm(resid(fit_bp)); qqline(resid(fit_bp))









Middle is straight, upper tail peels upward. Keep that in mind

title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
text:
Q-Q gallery with known truth
Four simulated samples; I wrote the generator, so the diagnosis is certain.


Code
set.seed(701)
qq_data <- bind_rows(
  tibble(panel = "Normal (n = 200)", z = rnorm(200)),
  tibble(panel = "Heavy tails (t, 3 df)", z = rt(200, df = 3)),
  tibble(panel = "Right skew (exponential)", z = rexp(200) - 1),
  tibble(panel = "Normal (n = 25)", z = rnorm(25))
)
qq_plot <- ggplot(qq_data, aes(sample = z)) +
  geom_qq(alpha = 0.6) + geom_qq_line() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Normal quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles")
