title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
text:
Reading the gallery

Normal, n = 200: hugs the line; this is your reference for boring
Heavy tails: both ends peel away (low end too low, high end too high); the most consequential departure, it breaks prediction intervals
Right skew: curved like a smile; short lower tail, long upper tail; common for costs, counts, rates
Normal, n = 25: genuinely normal, yet the ends wobble; small samples always look a bit ragged, so do not over-read tails at small n

title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
text:
Shapiro-Wilk: the formal test

shapiro.test(resid(fit_bp))


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  resid(fit_bp)
W = 0.96701, p-value < 2.2e-16



W = 0.967, p = 1.8 \times 10^{-21}: overwhelming rejection for our BP model
So is the model ruined? The Q-Q plot showed a moderate right skew and n = 2,088. Hold that thought

title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
section: Normality tests mislead at large n
text:
Normality tests mislead at large n

set.seed(2026)
close_to_normal <- rt(5000, df = 15)   # nearly normal
clearly_heavy  <- rt(30, df = 3)       # genuinely heavy-tailed
c(big_n_p = shapiro.test(close_to_normal)$p.value,
  small_n_p = shapiro.test(clearly_heavy)$p.value)

     big_n_p    small_n_p 
5.205110e-07 1.412366e-01 



t_{15}, n = 5,000: looks just like a normal, yet p \approx 5 \times 10^{-7}: rejected
t_3, n = 30: the tails that wreck prediction intervals, yet p \approx 0.14: waved through
The test rejects when it matters least and passes when it matters most; the Q-Q plot gets the final word

title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
text:
When normality actually matters



Situation
How much normality matters




Prediction intervals (any n)
A lot: PIs use the error tails


CIs and t tests, small n
Considerably


CIs and t tests, large n
Barely: the CLT rescues \hat\beta


Point estimates
Not at all for unbiasedness




Our BP model (n = 2,088): age-slope CIs are trustworthy despite Shapiro; individual PIs inherit the skew

title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
text:
Correlated errors
Assumption 3: knowing one error tells you nothing about another. Violated by time order (this month resembles last month), clusters (counties in the same state), repeated measures (same person twice).


Code
set.seed(2026)
n <- 60
t_idx <- 1:n
e <- as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.7), n = n, sd = 2))
y <- 50 + 0.3 * t_idx + e   # e.g., a monthly clinic caseload with a trend
fit_t <- lm(y ~ t_idx)
plot(t_idx, resid(fit_t), type = "b",
     xlab = "Time order", ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
text:
Residuals in time order










Slow waves: neighboring months are alike
Each month adds less information than the SE assumes

title: Week 7A: Normality and Independence
text:
Durbin-Watson, briefly

car::durbinWatsonTest(fit_t)

 lag Autocorrelation D-W Statistic p-value
   1       0.6658386      0.561717       0
 Alternative hypothesis: rho != 0



The Durbin-Watson statistic near 2 means no serial correlation; here it is about 0.56 with estimated autocorrelation 0.67: strong
Know the name and the plot (residuals vs time order); details belong to a time series course
Our data are cross-sectional: serial correlation rarely arises. The quieter cousin, clustering (counties in a state share policy), is beyond this course: acknowledge it in write-ups

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
This week’s question
Which socioeconomic conditions predict a county’s uninsured rate, and can we trust the coefficients we get?
The catch: income, poverty, and education all move together across counties. Today is about what that does to a regression.


Code
income_plot <- ggplot(soc, aes(median_income, uninsured)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Median household income ($)", y = "Uninsured (%)")

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
Income and the uninsured rate










Higher income, lower uninsured rate, with wide scatter

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
Warm-up: units change nothing real
Same model, income in dollars vs thousands of dollars:

m_dollars <- lm(uninsured ~ median_income, data = soc)
m_thousands <- lm(uninsured ~ I(median_income / 1000), data = soc)
rbind(dollars = summary(m_dollars)$coef[2, ],
      thousands = summary(m_thousands)$coef[2, ])

               Estimate   Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
dollars   -0.0001068598 7.073478e-06 -15.10711 1.576695e-47
thousands -0.1068598127 7.073478e-03 -15.10711 1.576695e-47



Slope and SE both scale by 1000; t is identical (-15.1)
R^2 (0.153), fitted values, and predictions: all identical
Rescaling changes the description, not the model. Use units readers feel: “per $1,000” beats “per dollar”

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
Standardization
Convert variables to z-scores: z = (x - \bar x)/s_x. Now every coefficient means “SDs of y per SD of x.”

coef(lm(scale(uninsured) ~ scale(poverty) + scale(hs_grad), data = soc))

   (Intercept) scale(poverty) scale(hs_grad) 
  1.450261e-15   6.002590e-02  -5.622091e-01 



Helps: comparing predictors in incompatible units; some journals require it
Hurts: “one SD of poverty” means nothing to a county commissioner; SDs are sample-specific, so results do not transfer across studies
Default in this course: natural units, chosen to be human-sized

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
section: Collinearity: the real problem of the day
text:
Collinearity: the real problem of the day
Predictors that carry overlapping information. In our county data:

soc |>
  select(poverty, median_income, per_capita_income, bachelors, hs_grad) |>
  cor() |> round(2)

                  poverty median_income per_capita_income bachelors hs_grad
poverty              1.00         -0.81             -0.74     -0.51   -0.66
median_income       -0.81          1.00              0.91      0.75    0.56
per_capita_income   -0.74          0.91              1.00      0.84    0.62
bachelors           -0.51          0.75              0.84      1.00    0.66
hs_grad             -0.66          0.56              0.62      0.66    1.00



The two income measures correlate at 0.91; per capita income and bachelors at 0.84; poverty and median income at -0.81
Each predictor is largely predictable from the others. The model must split credit among near-duplicates

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
Why collinearity inflates variance
R_j^2: the R^2 from regressing x_j on the other predictors.
\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat\beta_j) = \frac{\hat\sigma^2}{(n-1) s_{x_j}^2} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}}_{\text{VIF}_j}

x_j unrelated to the others: R_j^2 = 0, VIF = 1, no inflation
Others predict x_j well: 1 - R_j^2 is tiny, the variance blows up
“Holding others fixed” needs x_j to vary alone: rare if collinear

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
VIF in practice

m_full <- lm(uninsured ~ poverty + median_income + per_capita_income +
               bachelors + hs_grad, data = soc)
vif(m_full)

          poverty     median_income per_capita_income         bachelors 
         4.960423          8.376958          8.785169          5.207017 
          hs_grad 
         2.809778 



Per capita income has VIF near 8.8: its coefficient’s SE is \sqrt{8.8} \approx 3 times what it would be with uncorrelated predictors
Rules of thumb: VIF above 5 deserves attention, above 10 is serious. Treat these as smoke detectors, not verdicts
car::vif() needs the fitted model, not the raw data: collinearity is a property of the predictor set

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
Watching a coefficient become unstable
The bachelors coefficient, as correlated predictors enter:

tibble(
  model = c("bachelors alone", "+ hs_grad", "+ poverty", "+ both incomes"),
  bachelors_coef = c(
    coef(lm(uninsured ~ bachelors, data = soc))["bachelors"],
    coef(lm(uninsured ~ bachelors + hs_grad, data = soc))["bachelors"],
    coef(lm(uninsured ~ bachelors + hs_grad + poverty, data = soc))["bachelors"],
    coef(m_full)["bachelors"])
) |> mutate(bachelors_coef = round(bachelors_coef, 3))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  model           bachelors_coef
  <chr>                    <dbl>
1 bachelors alone         -0.156
2 + hs_grad                0.007
3 + poverty                0.011
4 + both incomes           0.127



Alone: -0.156. Full model: +0.127. The sign flips

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
Reading the sign flip

Alone, more college graduates go with fewer uninsured; adjusted for its correlated neighbors, the sign reverses
Neither number is “wrong”: they answer different adjusted questions
The instability warns that the data cannot cleanly separate these predictors

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
What collinearity does NOT do

m2 <- lm(uninsured ~ bachelors + hs_grad, data = soc)
c(r2_small = summary(m2)$r.squared, r2_full = summary(m_full)$r.squared,
  cor_of_predictions = cor(predict(m2), predict(m_full)))

          r2_small            r2_full cor_of_predictions 
         0.3621461          0.3898017          0.9638735 



Collinearity does not bias predictions: the small and full models’ fitted values correlate at 0.96, and the full model’s R^2 (0.39) is honest
It does not violate any least squares assumption; estimates remain unbiased
It widens coefficient CIs and destabilizes individual coefficients. If your goal is prediction, relax; if your goal is interpreting \hat\beta_j, worry

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
What to do about it

Drop one of a near-duplicate pair (keep the one your question is about): simplest and usually right
Combine overlapping predictors into one index (an SES score, a sum, a principal component) when they measure one construct
Accept with caution: keep everything, report the wide CIs, and refuse to interpret individual coefficients from the tangled block
What does not work: collecting more of the same kind of data helps only slowly; the confidence region is long and thin in a direction the data cannot see

title: Week 8A: Rescaling and Collinearity
text:
Think-pair-share (2 min)
A colleague models county uninsured rates with both median_income and per_capita_income (r = 0.91) and finds neither is significant, though each is highly significant alone.

What happened?
They conclude “income does not matter once you have both measures.” Fix that sentence.
Their boss only wants uninsured-rate predictions for next year. Does the collinearity problem block that use?
